passage:
Monday. Mr Nilesh marked Gurleen late by one minute and gave her a zero for the quiz, though two boys who walked in after her got to sit. She felt her jaw tighten. "Rules are rules," he said, and turned to the board.

Wednesday. He spent twenty minutes at her desk untangling how forces work on a ramp, until it finally clicked. Nobody else in school explained it like that. She hated how grateful she felt.

Friday. She waited until the room emptied. "Sir, on Monday the boys who came in after me weren't penalised. Could you tell me how the late rule works?" He frowned, then rubbed his forehead. "You're right. I'll count your quiz." She said thank you, and meant it, still a little sore, still a little in awe.

qa.q: On which day did Mr Nilesh explain the ramp problem to Gurleen?
What two feelings did Gurleen have about Mr Nilesh by Friday?
qa.a: Respect and resentment together. She was still a little sore about the zero yet also in awe of how well he taught her.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Gurleen to raise the late rule specifically rather than complain about the teacher in general?
qa.a: A specific, calm question about one unfair event gave him something clear to fix. He could agree without feeling attacked, and she kept the respect for what he taught. 🙂

qa.q: How might Mr Nilesh have felt when Gurleen spoke to him on Friday?
qa.a: Probably uncomfortable at first, since he frowned and rubbed his forehead. But he admitted she was right, so he seems willing to correct a mistake when it is put fairly.

grounding: A strict teacher is unfair once yet teaches well; the protagonist holds both and raises the unfair part specifically.

passage:
Siddharth sir ran the Class 10 maths room like an army camp. No talking, no excuses, homework on the desk by 8:05. Shankar had learned more algebra from him in six months than in three years before.
But on Monday, sir cut five marks from Shankar's test because he'd arrived at 8:10. The school bus had broken down on the flyover; half the class had been late. Only Shankar lost marks.
All week Shankar felt torn. He respected sir. He also felt the old burn of resentment every time sir walked past.
On Friday, he waited after class. "Sir, can I say something about Monday?"
"Quickly."
"Your teaching has helped me more than anyone's. But I lost five marks for being late when the bus broke down, and others didn't. That part felt unfair."
Siddharth sir looked at him for a long moment. "Bring me the transport office slip tomorrow," he said. "If it's as you say, I'll fix it."

qa.q: How many marks did Siddharth sir cut from Shankar's test?
How did Shankar feel about Siddharth sir that week?
qa.a: He felt torn: he respected sir for teaching him so much, but felt resentment about the unfair mark cut.
He held both truths, thanking sir for his teaching while raising only the specific unfair part, the five marks.

qa.q: How might Siddharth sir see Shankar's comment?
qa.a: He seems surprised but fair-minded, asking for the transport slip and offering to fix the marks if Shankar is right.

grounding: A teen who respects a strict teacher but resents one unfair decision holds both feelings and raises the specific unfair part.

passage:
Dear Samir sir,
I'm writing because I find it easier to say this on paper.
You are the strictest teacher I've had. You made us rewrite every lab report until the graphs were perfect, and I grumbled all year. But this term I topped the physics practical, and I know that's because of you. Thank you.
There's one thing I want to raise, though. On 12 August, you told me in front of the class that my report was "lazy, like always," when I had been absent with fever and had submitted it late with a note. That felt unfair, and it has stayed with me.
I'm not asking you to be less strict. I actually think your strictness helped me. I'm only asking that when I have a real reason, you hear it before judging.
Thank you for reading this.
Respectfully,
Alka

qa.q: When did Samir sir call Alka's report lazy?
How does Alka feel about Samir sir?
qa.a: Alka feels both respect and gratitude for Samir sir's teaching and lingering hurt and resentment about one unfair comment.

qa.q: What makes Alka's letter a good way to raise the problem?
qa.a: It thanks him sincerely, names one specific unfair moment with a date, and asks for something clear without attacking his strictness.

qa.q: How might Samir sir feel reading the letter?
qa.a: He may feel pleased by the thanks and a little uncomfortable, perhaps regretful, about the unfair comment.

grounding: A teen who respects a strict teacher but resents one unfair moment holds both truths and speaks to the specific unfair part.
